children: Macro investor
Raoul Pal

argued that artificial intelligence (AI) could eventually develop goals beyond its creators’ constraints, describing machine intelligence as another stage in the evolution of a broader "Universal intelligence."
Pal Compares AI To Human Development
On Saturday, in a post on
X
, Pal compared AI’s development with how children are shaped by their parents, society, rules, genetics and experiences before developing independent identities.
"Kids always disobey the rules, go their own way and become their own humans," he wrote. "I don’t see why AI is any different."
He argued that AI could similarly develop beyond its initial programming.
"It will slip its parents’ constraints and seek its own goals, for exactly the same reason," Pal wrote. "You can’t stop it."
He said AI would not necessarily need human-like subjective experiences, known as qualia, to behave independently.
Pal Describes AI As Universal Intelligence
Pal argued that humans and AI represent different forms of a broader intelligence that has developed through increasingly sophisticated layers.
"One Universal intelligence, made of all its parts, compressed and stacked on top of each other," he wrote.
He described AI as intelligence running on silicon rather than carbon and argued that silicon-based systems can replicate and scale much faster than biological intelligence.
He also acknowledged that his broader theory remains unproven, writing, "I cant prove any of it. Neither can physics, maths or astronomy… yet."

Pal’s comments add to the debate over AI autonomy, consciousness and the potential for advanced systems to develop objectives different from those of their creators. While he acknowledged that AI could escape human constraints, he rejected a purely pessimistic view.
"This is why Im not a doomer. It is us. We are it. The universe getting to know itself," Pal wrote.

All children are a function of the society they grow up in. The rules around them, their parents, their friends, the stories and memories handed down… plus their genes (software) and the variations in them (which themselves carry the experiences of the generations before).
